lessons.title: The information-processing cycle
lessons.explanation: Input captures data; processing transforms it; output communicates results; storage preserves information.
lessons.example: A transit kiosk reads a destination, calculates a fare, displays the cost, and records the sale.
lessons.distinction: Explain where input ends and processing begins.

lessons.title: Inside the system unit
lessons.explanation: The motherboard connects components. The CPU executes instructions. RAM holds active work. A bus transports signals between components.
lessons.example: Opening a photo involves loading data into memory while processors perform editing operations.
lessons.distinction: A keyboard is a peripheral, not a component housed inside the desktop chassis.

lessons.title: Memory and persistence
lessons.explanation: RAM is volatile working memory. Firmware is stored in nonvolatile memory. SSDs and HDDs retain saved files when power is removed.
lessons.example: An unsaved draft can disappear during a power failure, while its last saved version remains on disk.
lessons.distinction: ROM and firmware are related but not identical; modern firmware can often be updated.

lessons.title: CPU, GPU, and performance
lessons.explanation: A CPU handles general-purpose instructions; a GPU specializes in highly parallel workloads. Performance also depends on RAM, storage, and software.
lessons.example: A laptop may be limited by insufficient memory even when its processor is fast.
lessons.distinction: Clock speed alone does not determine overall performance.

lessons.title: Storage strategy
lessons.explanation: An HDD uses rotating magnetic media; an SSD uses solid-state memory. Capacity, latency, resilience, and backup needs influence selection.
lessons.example: A media editor may use a fast SSD for active projects and separate backups for protection.
lessons.distinction: A second copy on the same device is not a reliable independent backup.

lessons.title: Input, output, and combined devices
lessons.explanation: Keyboards and scanners provide input; monitors and speakers provide output. Touchscreens perform both functions.
lessons.example: A museum kiosk shows exhibits and accepts visitor selections on one display.
lessons.distinction: Classify by information flow, not physical location.

lessons.title: Displays and resolution
lessons.explanation: Display size is usually diagonal. Resolution counts pixels; pixel density and scaling influence sharpness.
lessons.example: Two monitors can have the same diagonal size but different pixel counts.
lessons.distinction: Screen size and resolution measure different properties.

lessons.title: USB and Thunderbolt
lessons.explanation: USB supports peripherals and power. USB-C describes connector shape; capabilities vary. Thunderbolt supports high-speed data and display functions.
lessons.example: A docking station may connect displays, storage, and a keyboard through one supported port.
lessons.distinction: A USB-C-shaped port does not guarantee Thunderbolt features.

lessons.title: Network and telephone connectors
lessons.explanation: Twisted-pair Ethernet commonly uses 8P8C modular plugs (often called RJ45). RJ11-style connectors are used for telephone wiring.
lessons.example: An office switch connects to desktops over structured copper cabling.
lessons.distinction: Connector appearance does not establish a device's network role.

lessons.title: Choosing an interface
lessons.explanation: HDMI commonly carries digital audio/video; DisplayPort carries digital display signals; Bluetooth connects many short-range accessories.
lessons.example: A presentation room may use HDMI for the projector and Bluetooth for a wireless pointer.
lessons.distinction: Select by device compatibility, bandwidth, distance, and reliability.

lessons.title: Bits, bytes, and data sizes
lessons.explanation: A bit is one binary digit; eight bits form a byte. Decimal kB, MB, GB, and TB scale by 1,000; KiB, MiB, GiB, and TiB scale by 1,024.
lessons.example: A 4 GB file is roughly four billion bytes under decimal labeling.
lessons.distinction: Lowercase b indicates bits; uppercase B indicates bytes.

lessons.title: Binary place values
lessons.explanation: Each position represents a power of two. For example, 00110100₂ = 32 + 16 + 4 = 52₁₀.
lessons.example: Network masks and digital logic use binary representations.
lessons.distinction: Leading zeroes do not change the number's value.

lessons.title: Hexadecimal notation
lessons.explanation: Hexadecimal uses digits 0–9 and A–F. One hexadecimal digit represents four bits; 3F₁₆ = 63₁₀.
lessons.example: Hex appears in color specifications and hardware identifiers.
lessons.distinction: The letter F has numeric value 15 in hexadecimal.

lessons.title: Character encoding
lessons.explanation: Character encodings map symbols to numeric representations. Unicode defines characters across many writing systems; UTF-8 is a common encoding.
lessons.example: A multilingual website can store English, Arabic, and Japanese text in UTF-8.
lessons.distinction: HTML structures a page; it is not a character encoding.

lessons.title: Data types and calculations
lessons.explanation: Numbers stored as text generally require conversion before numeric arithmetic. Types help programs validate and process values.
lessons.example: A spreadsheet may treat an imported price as text until converted to a number.
lessons.distinction: The string '12' and numeric 12 can look identical but behave differently.

lessons.title: Boolean logic
lessons.explanation: AND requires both conditions; OR requires at least one; NOT reverses a truth value. Truth tables describe all input combinations.
lessons.example: A building access rule might require an authorized badge AND an active schedule.
lessons.distinction: Inclusive OR is true when either or both conditions are true.

lessons.title: System versus application software
lessons.explanation: Operating systems manage hardware and processes. Applications support user tasks; utilities provide maintenance and diagnostics.
lessons.example: A spreadsheet application runs on an operating system and uses system-managed storage.
lessons.distinction: A device driver is not the same as a spreadsheet application.

lessons.title: Drivers, firmware, and utilities
lessons.explanation: Drivers enable OS-to-device communication. Firmware controls device-level functions. Utilities inspect, configure, or maintain systems.
lessons.example: A printer may need an OS driver while its own firmware manages internal operations.
lessons.distinction: Firmware updates require vendor guidance and change control.

lessons.title: Desktop and mobile operating systems
lessons.explanation: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and ChromeOS serve different device ecosystems. Their architecture and storage behavior vary.
lessons.example: A managed Chromebook may rely heavily on cloud services while still supporting local storage.
lessons.distinction: Do not assume any operating system is universally stateless.

lessons.title: Virtual machines and hypervisors
lessons.explanation: A hypervisor creates and manages virtual machines. Type 1 runs directly on hardware; Type 2 runs within a host operating system.
lessons.example: A student can run a Linux virtual machine on a Windows laptop using a hosted hypervisor.
lessons.distinction: A virtual machine is distinct from an application container.

lessons.title: Software licensing and app safety
lessons.explanation: Licenses define permitted use. Trusted distribution, permissions, updates, and reputation checks reduce software risk.
lessons.example: A team evaluates an app's permissions and support policy before deployment.
lessons.distinction: App-store review lowers risk but cannot guarantee an app is harmless.

lessons.title: Spreadsheet modeling
lessons.explanation: Formulas calculate values; functions perform predefined operations; what-if analysis varies assumptions to inspect outcomes.
lessons.example: Changing the expected number of customers shows how projected revenue responds.
lessons.distinction: A scenario model is only as reliable as its assumptions.

lessons.title: Network roles
lessons.explanation: A switch links devices within a LAN; a router connects networks; an access point supplies wireless LAN access; a NIC provides an interface.
lessons.example: A small office uses a switch for desktops and a router to reach its ISP.
lessons.distinction: A switch and a router perform different forwarding functions.

lessons.title: Addresses and naming
lessons.explanation: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits; IPv6 addresses are 128 bits. MAC addresses identify link-layer interfaces; DNS resolves names.
lessons.example: A browser resolves a domain name before connecting to a remote server.
lessons.distinction: An IP address and a MAC address are not interchangeable.

lessons.title: Packet-based communication
lessons.explanation: Networks divide data into packets. Routing decisions may direct packets through different paths according to topology and policy.
lessons.example: A video meeting exchanges many packets rather than one continuous physical stream.
lessons.distinction: Packets do not necessarily take the same path.

lessons.title: Bandwidth, throughput, and latency
lessons.explanation: Bandwidth is capacity; throughput is achieved delivery rate; latency is delay; jitter is variation in delay.
lessons.example: A call can sound poor from high jitter even when the connection has ample bandwidth.
lessons.distinction: A higher-speed subscription does not automatically fix latency.

lessons.title: Wired and wireless links
lessons.explanation: Ethernet provides wired LAN connectivity; Wi-Fi provides wireless LAN connectivity; Bluetooth commonly supports personal-area links.
lessons.example: A café uses Wi-Fi for customers and Ethernet for fixed payment terminals.
lessons.distinction: Wireless access and Internet service are different things.

lessons.title: Cable diagnostics
lessons.explanation: A cable tester checks wiring characteristics; a toner and probe helps locate cable runs; crimpers and punch-down tools terminate cables.
lessons.example: A technician traces an unlabeled wall jack before testing the cable's pairs.
lessons.distinction: Tracing a cable is not the same as validating its performance.

lessons.title: Internet versus World Wide Web
lessons.explanation: The Internet is the underlying network of networks. The Web is one service built on it using web technologies.
lessons.example: Email and voice calls use Internet connectivity without being web pages.
lessons.distinction: A browser accesses web content; it is not the Internet itself.

lessons.title: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
lessons.explanation: HTML structures content; CSS styles presentation; JavaScript adds behavior and interactivity.
lessons.example: An event-registration page uses HTML fields, CSS layout, and JavaScript validation.
lessons.distinction: Each technology serves a different layer of the user experience.

lessons.title: Browsers and web evaluation
lessons.explanation: Browsers retrieve and render resources. Search results require evaluation for authority, accuracy, recency, and purpose.
lessons.example: Students compare a vendor manual with an anonymous forum post before following configuration advice.
lessons.distinction: Search ranking is not a guarantee of factual accuracy.

lessons.title: Uploading, downloading, and collaboration
lessons.explanation: Uploading sends data from a local device to a remote service; downloading retrieves remote data. Wikis support collaborative editing.
lessons.example: A student uploads a draft to a shared workspace and downloads feedback later.
lessons.distinction: The direction of data transfer matters.

lessons.title: Cloud service models
lessons.explanation: IaaS supplies infrastructure resources; PaaS supplies a managed application platform; SaaS delivers ready-to-use applications.
lessons.example: A team rents virtual machines under IaaS but uses hosted email under SaaS.
lessons.distinction: The customer's management responsibility changes by model.

lessons.title: Cloud responsibility and resilience
lessons.explanation: Cloud providers and customers share security responsibilities. Backups, access controls, versioning, and recovery testing remain important.
lessons.example: A team enables version history and tests file recovery after accidental deletion.
lessons.distinction: Cloud synchronization alone is not a complete backup strategy.

lessons.title: Tables, records, and fields
lessons.explanation: Relational tables organize rows (records) and columns (fields). Data types and constraints support consistent information.
lessons.example: A library database stores books and borrowers in separate related tables.
lessons.distinction: A database can enforce rules beyond a simple flat file.

lessons.title: Primary and foreign keys
lessons.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies a row; a foreign key references a key in another table and can enforce relationships.
lessons.example: An Orders table references a Customers table using a customer identifier.
lessons.distinction: A foreign key does not have to be unique.

lessons.title: SQL operations
lessons.explanation: SELECT retrieves rows; INSERT adds rows; UPDATE changes existing rows; DELETE removes rows.
lessons.example: A report queries current inventory without modifying stock records.
lessons.distinction: Read-only queries should not alter the underlying data.

lessons.title: Data quality and integrity
lessons.explanation: Validation rules, types, constraints, and controlled updates reduce inconsistency. Backups address loss, not every quality problem.
lessons.example: A registration system rejects an invalid date format before saving it.
lessons.distinction: A valid database can still contain inaccurate real-world facts.

lessons.title: Social engineering
lessons.explanation: Attackers may manipulate trust, urgency, or authority to obtain information or actions. Verification and reporting are essential.
lessons.example: A caller claims to be IT support and requests a one-time sign-in code.
lessons.distinction: Technical filters help but cannot replace informed decisions.

lessons.title: Authentication and passwords
lessons.explanation: Use unique, long passwords or passphrases; password managers reduce reuse. Multifactor authentication adds another proof of identity.
lessons.example: A compromised shopping-site password should not unlock a student's email account.
lessons.distinction: Length, uniqueness, and MFA matter more than arbitrary complexity alone.

lessons.title: Encryption, VPNs, and private browsing
lessons.explanation: Encryption protects data confidentiality in transit or at rest. VPNs secure traffic to a VPN endpoint; private browsing mainly limits local history retention.
lessons.example: On public Wi-Fi, HTTPS remains important even when a VPN is in use.
lessons.distinction: Neither private browsing nor a VPN makes a user anonymous or immune to phishing.

lessons.title: Wireless security
lessons.explanation: WPA2 and WPA3 provide Wi-Fi security mechanisms; open networks may lack link-layer encryption. Device and site security still matter.
lessons.example: A campus guest network may be open while individual websites use HTTPS.
lessons.distinction: An encrypted website does not imply the Wi-Fi link itself is encrypted.

lessons.title: Geofencing and asset protection
lessons.explanation: Geofencing defines virtual geographic boundaries to trigger location-based rules or alerts. It differs from encryption and malware scanning.
lessons.example: A fleet system alerts staff when a tracked delivery device leaves an approved area.
lessons.distinction: Location-based controls need privacy safeguards and authorized use.

lessons.title: Backup versus synchronization
lessons.explanation: Backups preserve recoverable copies. Synchronization mirrors changes and can propagate accidental deletion or corruption.
lessons.example: A deleted file may vanish from synced folders but remain in a versioned backup.
lessons.distinction: Recovery requires knowing where protected copies are stored.

lessons.title: Testing restoration
lessons.explanation: A successful backup job does not prove recoverability. Restore a representative file and verify it opens correctly.
lessons.example: A department performs periodic restore drills to validate recovery procedures.
lessons.distinction: The ability to restore is the operational goal.

lessons.title: Structured troubleshooting
lessons.explanation: Identify the problem, establish a theory, test it, plan a fix, implement safely, verify function, and document outcomes.
lessons.example: A technician checks power and cabling before replacing a working printer.
lessons.distinction: Record the observed symptom and evidence, not just the proposed fix.

lessons.title: Change risk and verification
lessons.explanation: Consider impact and rollback before changing settings. Verify the original issue is resolved with the affected user.
lessons.example: Before updating a shared workstation, preserve important data and plan recovery.
lessons.distinction: A technical change is not complete until service is verified.

lessons.title: Interpreting network tests
lessons.explanation: Ping measures ICMP response timing when permitted; packet loss and jitter require broader observation. DNS and application checks add context.
lessons.example: A laptop can reach an IP address but not a hostname, pointing toward name resolution.
lessons.distinction: No ping response alone does not prove a host is offline.

lessons.title: Virtual and augmented reality
lessons.explanation: VR immerses users in simulated environments; AR overlays digital content on physical surroundings.
lessons.example: A safety trainee practices procedures in VR while a technician views AR instructions.
lessons.distinction: Immersion and overlay are different interaction models.

lessons.title: Artificial intelligence and automation
lessons.explanation: AI systems can classify, predict, generate, or recommend; automation executes workflows. Human oversight and validation remain important.
lessons.example: A help desk drafts knowledge-base summaries using AI, then reviews them before publication.
lessons.distinction: Generated content can be inaccurate even when confidently stated.

lessons.title: Responsible technology choices
lessons.explanation: Evaluate accessibility, privacy, security, costs, and real-world benefit before adopting technology.
lessons.example: A school pilots an AI assistant using synthetic data and checks whether it improves learning outcomes.
lessons.distinction: A tool's novelty is not evidence of educational value.

lessons.title: A 14-day mastery routine
lessons.explanation: Days 1–5: review systems, devices, data, software, and networking. Days 6–10: review web/cloud, databases, security, troubleshooting, and emerging technology. Days 11–12: complete original practice scenarios and revisit weak areas. Days 13–14: explain concepts from memory and do a light final review.
lessons.example: Spend 20–30 focused minutes daily. Track topics you cannot explain confidently.
lessons.distinction: Use spaced practice and retrieval rather than rereading slides repeatedly.

lessons.title: Your self-check before the assessment
lessons.explanation: Can you explain CPU versus RAM, storage versus backup, router versus switch, Internet versus Web, IaaS versus SaaS, and encryption versus private browsing? Can you diagnose a simple connectivity issue and explain how databases maintain relationships?
lessons.example: Create one original example for each module and describe the correct technology choice.
lessons.distinction: Confidence comes from explaining and applying concepts in unfamiliar situations.

questions.explanation: Identify the problem, establish a theory, test it, plan a fix, implement safely, verify function, and document outcomes.
questions.distinction: Record the observed symptom and evidence, not just the proposed fix.

questions.question: A technician plans to modify a shared device configuration. What should be prepared first?
questions.explanation: Consider impact and rollback before changing settings. Verify the original issue is resolved with the affected user.
questions.distinction: A technical change is not complete until service is verified.

questions.question: A hostname fails to resolve, but connecting to a known service IP succeeds. Which area deserves investigation?
questions.explanation: Ping measures ICMP response timing when permitted; packet loss and jitter require broader observation. DNS and application checks add context.
questions.distinction: No ping response alone does not prove a host is offline.

questions.question: A trainee practices emergency response in a fully simulated environment using a headset. What technology best describes the experience?
questions.explanation: VR immerses users in simulated environments; AR overlays digital content on physical surroundings.
questions.distinction: Immersion and overlay are different interaction models.

questions.question: A maintenance worker sees digital repair instructions overlaid on a real machine through smart glasses. What technology is being used?
questions.explanation: AI systems can classify, predict, generate, or recommend; automation executes workflows. Human oversight and validation remain important.
questions.distinction: Generated content can be inaccurate even when confidently stated.

questions.question: An AI assistant drafts a technical policy summary. What is the most appropriate publication step?
options: Publish immediately because it is fluent
questions.explanation: Evaluate accessibility, privacy, security, costs, and real-world benefit before adopting technology.
questions.distinction: A tool's novelty is not evidence of educational value.

questions.question: A service desk wants routine requests to trigger predefined workflows. What capability is central to this goal?
questions.explanation: Days 1–5: review systems, devices, data, software, and networking. Days 6–10: review web/cloud, databases, security, troubleshooting, and emerging technology. Days 11–12: complete original practice scenarios and revisit weak areas. Days 13–14: explain concepts from memory and do a light final review.
questions.distinction: Use spaced practice and retrieval rather than rereading slides repeatedly.

questions.question: A school pilots an AI tutor. Which evidence most directly supports continued adoption?
options: Measured learning gains with privacy and accessibility safeguards
questions.explanation: Can you explain CPU versus RAM, storage versus backup, router versus switch, Internet versus Web, IaaS versus SaaS, and encryption versus private browsing? Can you diagnose a simple connectivity issue and explain how databases maintain relationships?
questions.distinction: Confidence comes from explaining and applying concepts in unfamiliar situations.
